title: Files, Errors & OOP
goal: Read and write text, JSON and CSV files, handle errors with try/except and raise your own, write clean code with classes, objects and the 4 pillars of OOP, and understand the basic use of generators and decorators — all from the point of view of ML data and models.

lessons.title: File handling — saving data for good
blocks: Data kept in a variable lives in **RAM**. Program closes, data is gone. If you want to keep data **permanently** (report, log, ML results), you have to write it to a **file**.
**What:** reading/writing files with Python — text, JSON, CSV
**Why:** the data stays even after the program closes
**When:** logs, loading config, data import/export, model results
**Where:** every real project — ERP data, ML training logs, reports

with open("report.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Cable 1: PASS\n")
    f.write("Cable 2: FAIL\n")

with open("report.txt", "r") as f:
    data = f.read()
print(data)
Understand the line: `open("report.txt", "w")` = open the file in **write mode**. `as f` = give the open file the name `f`. `f.write(...)` = write. `\n` is for a new line; it is not added by itself.
**Why `with`?** As soon as the `with` block ends, the file **closes by itself**, even if an error happens. If a file is not closed, the data may not be fully saved, or the file may stay locked.
`with` is an automatic door: you go in, do the work, come out, and the door shuts by itself. In the old way you had to remember `f.close()` yourself — forget it and the door stays open.

with open("report.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Cable 1: PASS\n")
    f.write("Cable 2: FAIL\n")
with open("report.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Cable 3: PASS\n")

with open("report.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())

Cable 1: PASS
Cable 2: FAIL
Cable 3: PASS
Read a big file line by line with `for line in f`. Only one line comes into memory at a time, so even a 5 GB log file works. `.strip()` removes the `\n` at the end.

with open("report.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Cable 1: PASS\nCable 2: FAIL\nCable 3: PASS\n")
with open("report.txt") as f:
    lines = f.read().splitlines()
passed = [l for l in lines if l.endswith("PASS")]
print(len(lines), len(passed))

Common mistake: a file opened in `"w"` mode loses its old data **immediately**, even if you write nothing. To add, use `"a"`. And in `"r"` mode, if the file is not found you get **FileNotFoundError**.
If you write Hindi/special characters, writing `open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8")` is a good habit. On Windows the default encoding is different and can give an error.

lessons.title: JSON and CSV — the real data of AI/ML
blocks: **JSON** = a text format that looks just like a Python dict/list. APIs, config files, LLM responses — all come in JSON. In AI/ML you will use it **the most**.

import json
cable = {"name": "5 Core", "price": 4500, "stock": True, "sizes": [10, 16]}

with open("cable.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(cable, f, indent=2)

with open("cable.json") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)
print(loaded["name"], loaded["sizes"][1])
print(type(loaded))
How to remember: **s = string**. `dumps`/`loads` work with text, `dump`/`load` work with a file.

import json
response = '{"status": "ok", "data": [{"id": 1, "score": 0.91}, {"id": 2, "score": 0.47}]}'
obj = json.loads(response)
print(obj["status"])
good = [d["id"] for d in obj["data"] if d["score"] > 0.5]
print(good)
print(json.dumps({"ok": True, "n": None}))
Look carefully at the last line: Python `True` → JSON `true`, `None` → `null`. In JSON, keys are always in **double quotes**.
**CSV** = Comma Separated Values. A table like Excel, in simple text. Each line is one row. Most datasets (Kaggle etc.) come as CSV.

import csv
rows = [["name", "city", "amount"], ["Rahul", "Delhi", 50000], ["Neha", "Jaipur", 20000]]
with open("leads.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerows(rows)

with open("leads.csv") as f:
    print(f.read().strip())

import csv
with open("leads.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["name", "city", "amount"])
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerow({"name": "Rahul", "city": "Delhi", "amount": 50000})
    w.writerow({"name": "Neha", "city": "Jaipur", "amount": 20000})

total = 0
with open("leads.csv") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row["name"], row["city"])
        total += int(row["amount"])
print("Total:", total)

Common mistake: **every value** from a CSV comes as a **string**, even `"50000"`. Do `int()` / `float()` before any maths. And when writing, pass `newline=""`, otherwise on Windows you get empty lines in between.
Later, in Stage 8, `pd.read_csv()` will do all of this in one line. But now you know what happens inside — that is exactly the difference that shows in an IQ.

lessons.title: Errors — save your program from crashing
blocks: When an error comes, the program **stops right there** (crash). In a real app the user may give wrong input, a file may be missing, an API may be down — the whole server should not go down.
**try / except** = "try this, and if something goes wrong, handle it."

Yeh number nahi hai
Program chalta raha

Result: 5.0
--- done ---
0 se divide nahi hota
--- done ---
`else` runs when **no error** came. `finally` runs **always** — that is why cleanup (closing a file, closing a DB connection) is written there.
**raise** = send an error yourself. When a function gets a wrong value, it is better to give a clear error than to quietly give a wrong result.
**Custom exception** = your own error class. Inherit from `Exception` (inheritance comes in the next lessons). Then the error's name itself tells what went wrong.

OK
Rejected: 7 sqmm standard size nahi hai
try/except is a safety net, like the net under a trapeze in a circus. A fall (error) can happen, but the show (program) goes on.
Common mistake: writing `except:` or `except Exception: pass` and hiding all errors. The bug will never be caught. Catch only the errors you **can handle**, and at least log a message.
In an ML pipeline: don't stop the whole training because of a bad row. Skip that row with `try/except` and count how many rows were bad.

lessons.title: OOP — class and object
blocks: **Class** = a map (blueprint). **Object** = the real thing built from that map. One map, many objects, each with its own values.

A house map says "3 rooms, 1 kitchen". The map itself is not a house. From that map you can build 10 houses — each house with a different colour and owner. At GEEP: the "Cable" class is the map, the cable on each drum is an object.

**Why?** Data (name, size, price) and the work on that data (calculate price, give discount) are tied together in one place. Big projects stay clean. And ML libraries (scikit-learn, PyTorch) are built fully on OOP: `model = LinearRegression()` is an object!

class Cable:
    def __init__(self, name, size, price):
        self.name = name
        self.size = size
        self.price = price

c1 = Cable("5 Core", 16, 4500)
c2 = Cable("3 Core", 10, 2600)
print(c1.name, c1.price)
print(c2.name, c2.price)
`__init__` (two underscores in front, two behind) = **constructor**. Whenever you write `Cable(...)`, it runs **by itself** and sets the starting values of the new object.

**`self` = "this object here".** When you write `c1 = Cable(...)`, Python runs `__init__(c1, ...)` inside, so `self = c1`. That is why `self.name = name` means `c1.name = "5 Core"`. You don't pass `self` yourself, Python does.
**Method** = a function inside a class. It works on the object's data.

class Cable:
    company = "GEEP"          # class attribute: same for all

    def __init__(self, name, price):
        self.name = name      # instance attribute: separate for each object
        self.price = price

    def discount(self, pct):
        self.price = round(self.price * (1 - pct / 100))

    def info(self):
        return f"{self.company} {self.name}: Rs {self.price}"

c1 = Cable("5 Core", 4500)
c2 = Cable("3 Core", 2600)
c1.discount(10)
print(c1.info())
print(c2.info())

GEEP 5 Core: Rs 4050
GEEP 3 Core: Rs 2600
Look carefully: `c1.discount(10)` changed only c1's price, no effect on c2. Every object keeps its own value.
**Dunder methods** (double underscore) = Python's special methods. With them your object starts working with built-in things: `print()`, `len()`, `+`, `==`.
Common mistake: forgetting to write `self` as the first parameter of a method → `TypeError: takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given`. And in `__str__` you must **return**, not `print`.
**Connection to ML:** every scikit-learn model is an object with `fit()` and `predict()`. We can build the same pattern ourselves:
Values created after `fit` have a `_` at the end of their name (like `mean_`, `coef_`) — this is a scikit-learn convention. You will see it in Stage 10.

lessons.title: The 4 pillars of OOP — A PIE
blocks: This surely comes in an IQ: "What are the four pillars of OOP?" Not just the names — say the **meaning + an example** of each. How to remember: **A PIE** — Abstraction, Polymorphism, Inheritance, Encapsulation.
**1. Encapsulation** — data and its work in one class, and stopping the data from being changed directly from outside. Changes happen only through methods, which check the rules.
ATM: you cannot take the money out of the machine by hand. Work happens only through buttons (deposit, withdraw), and the machine checks whether there is enough balance.

1500
Private hai, bahar se nahi dikhta

Naming rules: `name` = public. `_name` = "it's internal, don't touch" (just a hint). `__name` = Python changes the name (name mangling), no direct access from outside. With `@property` you can read it like an attribute, but you cannot set it.
**2. Inheritance** — a child class takes all the properties and methods of the parent class, and can add its own new ones. You don't have to write the code again.

Akash earns 50000
Akash manages 5 people
True
`super()` = the parent. `super().__init__(name, salary)` runs the parent's constructor. **is-a test:** Is a Manager an Employee? Yes → inheritance is right.
**3. Polymorphism** — poly = many, morph = form. **Same method name, each object does the work its own way.** When a child rewrites a parent's method, it is called **method overriding**.

Paid 500 via UPI
Paid 500 via Card
Paid 500
3 2

The play button on a remote: press it on the TV and you get a channel, on the music system you get a song. Same button, the work depends on the device. `len()` also works on both strings and lists — that is polymorphism too.
**4. Abstraction** — show only what is needed, hide the complexity inside. In Python an **abstract class (ABC)** is a rule-book: "every child must create this method".

42
Abstract class ka object nahi banta

IQ trap: Encapsulation vs Abstraction. Encapsulation hides **data** (you can't change the balance directly). Abstraction hides **complexity** (you don't need to understand the engine to drive a car; just call `model.fit()`, don't look at the maths inside).

lessons.title: Generators and Decorators — intro
blocks: These two are favourite advanced IQ questions. People know the names but can't explain them. Make sure you understand both well.
**Generator** = give values **one by one**, don't build them all in memory at once. `yield` instead of `return`.
List = make 100 cups of tea in advance and keep them (takes space and effort). Generator = make one cup only when someone asks.

def simple():
    print("Start")
    yield 1
    print("Beech")
    yield 2

g = simple()
print(next(g))
print(next(g))
try:
    next(g)
except StopIteration:
    print("Khatam")

import sys
lst = [x for x in range(100000)]
gen = (x for x in range(100000))
print(sys.getsizeof(lst) > 100000, sys.getsizeof(gen) < 1000)
print(sum(gen))

The list took lakhs of bytes, the generator a few hundred bytes — same values. **In ML:** reading a big CSV/log file line by line, and feeding data in **batches** during training — both are done with generators.
Common mistake: a generator runs **only once**. If you do `list(g)` again, you get an empty `[]`.
**Decorator** = a **wrapper (envelope)** around a function. Add extra work to the real function without changing it: logging, timing, login check, retry.
Gift wrap: the gift (function) is the same, we just put a wrapper on top that does extra work.
Writing `@log` = the same as writing `add = log(add)`. A function is also a value; you can give it to another function and get a new function back.

Add `@functools.wraps(func)` so the wrapped function does not lose its name and docstring. You will see these decorators every day: `@app.get("/")` in FastAPI, `@property` and `@staticmethod` in classes.

teach.say: A variable's data is gone as soon as the program closes. To keep it for good, write it to a file: open, write or read, close.
Remember three modes. r reads, w writes and wipes the old data, and a adds at the end. with closes the file by itself.
JSON is text that looks just like a dict. dump and load work with a file, dumps and loads with a string. s means string.
A CSV is a table. DictReader turns each row into a dict. Just keep in mind, every value comes as a string.
teach.code:
for row in csv.DictReader(f):
    total += int(row["amount"])

teach.say: An error means the program crashes. Put risky work in try, handle it in except, else runs when all is fine, and finally always runs.
If you get a wrong value, raise an error yourself. You can also make your own error class by inheriting from Exception.
A class is the map, the object is the real house. init runs as soon as the object is created, and self means this object here.
Dunder methods let an object work with built-in things: str for print, len for len.
Four pillars, A PIE: Abstraction, Polymorphism, Inheritance, Encapsulation. Learn one example of each by heart.
A generator gives one value at a time with yield, saving memory. A decorator puts a wrapper around a function, without changing the function.

practice.solution:
class MinMaxScaler:
    def fit(self, data):
        self.min_ = min(data)
        self.max_ = max(data)
        return self

    def transform(self, data):
        span = self.max_ - self.min_
        return [round((x - self.min_) / span, 2) for x in data]

    def __str__(self):
        return f"MinMaxScaler(min={self.min_}, max={self.max_})"

scaler = MinMaxScaler().fit([10, 20, 30, 50])
print(scaler)
print(scaler.transform([10, 20, 30, 50]))
print(scaler.transform([40, 60]))

quiz.q: What does `open("data.txt", "w")` do to an existing file?
o: Wipes old data and writes new
quiz.why: "w" mode empties the file. To add, use "a".

quiz.q: Biggest benefit of `with open(...) as f:`?
o: File closes by itself after the block, even on error
quiz.why: with is a context manager; as soon as the block ends (even with an error) the file is closed.

quiz.q: How do you turn a JSON string (text) into a Python dict?
quiz.why: s = string: `loads` reads from text, `load` reads from a file object.

quiz.q: What is the type of `row["amount"]` from `csv.DictReader`?
quiz.why: CSV is a text file; every value comes as a string, so for maths you need int()/float().
else runs only when the try block finished without an exception.
Asking a dict for a key it does not have with `[ ]` gives KeyError.

quiz.q: What is `self` in a class method?
quiz.why: self points to the object the method was called on; Python passes it automatically.

quiz.q: Which method shows custom text on `print(obj)`?
quiz.why: Whatever string `__str__` returns is what print() shows.

quiz.q: How do you run the parent's constructor in a child class?
quiz.why: `super()` gives the parent class; calling its `__init__` sets the parent's attributes.

quiz.q: What is true about a generator?
o: Builds all values in memory first
Gives one value at a time with yield and iterates only once
Can only be made inside a class
quiz.why: yield pauses the function and gives one value; once a generator is finished it does not run again.

iq.q: What is the `with` statement and why is it used with files?
iq.a: `with` uses a context manager: it opens the resource when entering the block (`__enter__`) and closes it when leaving (`__exit__`), even if an exception happens. For files, DB connections and locks this prevents resource leaks. With `with open("a.txt") as f:` you never have to write `f.close()`.

`json.load(f)` reads JSON from a file object and gives a Python object. `json.loads(s)` does it from a JSON string. In the same way, `dump(obj, f)` writes to a file and `dumps(obj)` returns a string. loads is used to parse API response text.

iq.q: try, except, else, finally — when does each one run?
iq.a: try holds the risky code. except runs when a matching exception comes. else runs when no exception came in try. finally always runs, so cleanup (closing a file/connection) is written there. You should catch specific exceptions, not a bare `except:`.

iq.q: How do you create a custom exception, and why?
iq.a: By inheriting from `Exception`: `class InvalidInput(Exception): pass`, then `raise InvalidInput("msg")`. The error's type itself tells what went wrong, and the caller can catch only that one without hiding other errors. Big projects create one base exception and its sub-classes.

iq.q: Difference between class and object? What are `__init__` and `self`?
iq.a: A class is a blueprint, an object is an instance made from that blueprint. `__init__` is the constructor that runs as soon as the object is created and sets initial values. `self` is a reference to the current object, so each object keeps its own separate data: `self.name = name`.

iq.q: Explain the 4 pillars of OOP with examples.
iq.a: Encapsulation: data + methods in one class, data private, like a balance that changes only through deposit/withdraw. Inheritance: the child takes the parent's features, like Manager(Employee). Polymorphism: the same method does different work in different objects, like pay() for UPI and Card. Abstraction: show only the needed interface, like an ABC where every model must create predict().

iq.q: What is the difference between Encapsulation and Abstraction?
iq.a: Encapsulation hides and protects data (private attributes, getters/property) so that no wrong value gets in. Abstraction hides the complexity of the implementation and gives only a simple interface (abstract classes, `model.fit()`). One is about 'what is hidden' (data), the other about 'how it works' (detail).

iq.q: Difference between a class attribute and an instance attribute?
iq.a: A class attribute is written in the class body and is shared by all objects (`company = "GEEP"`). An instance attribute is set with `self.x` in `__init__` and is separate for each object. A mutable class attribute (like a list) gets shared by all objects and causes bugs, so keep per-object data in instance attributes.

`__str__` gives user-friendly text and is used by `print()` and `str()`. `__repr__` is an unambiguous representation for the developer, shown in the console and while debugging, ideally such that the object could be rebuilt from it: `Cable('5 Core', 4500)`. If there is no `__str__`, Python uses `__repr__`.

iq.q: What is a generator, and yield vs return?
iq.a: A generator gives values lazily, one by one, with `yield`; it does not build the whole list in memory. `yield` pauses the function and gives a value, and next time resumes from the same place; `return` ends the function. Ideal for reading big files and feeding data batches in ML training. A generator can be iterated only once.

iq.q: What is a decorator? Give one real use.
iq.a: A decorator is a function that takes another function, wraps it and returns a new function, without changing the original code. Writing `@timer` = `func = timer(func)`. Uses: logging, measuring execution time, auth check, retry, caching (`@functools.lru_cache`). `functools.wraps` keeps the original name/docstring.

iq.q: How is scikit-learn's fit/predict design connected to OOP?
iq.a: Every model is a class; `model = LinearRegression()` creates an object. `fit(X, y)` stores the values learned from data in the object's attributes (`coef_`, `intercept_`), and `predict(X)` uses those same values. All models follow the same interface (polymorphism), so swapping one model for another is a one-line change.
